text: Training leaves you with a pile of experiment runs. Deployment needs something more disciplined: a named, versioned model that an endpoint can point to. That is the model registry, and every lesson in this chapter starts from it.

Per Microsoft Learn, a registered model is a logical container for the files that make up your model. You identify it by name and version. Register again under the same name, and the version number increments. You can attach tags and a description, and the registry keeps metadata such as which run trained it.

I ran the idea locally with an M L flow registry. I logged two pipelines, a logistic regression and gradient boosting, and registered both as churn model. The registry printed version one, then version two. Each version points back to its run, so the lineage shows A U C point seven nine three four for version one and point seven eight seven for version two.

In Azure Machine Learning, you build a Model object with a path, a name, and a type, then call create or update. The path can be a local file, a datastore, a job output, or an M L flow run URI. Using the run form records lineage back to the run. This is illustrative; I checked the class names locally, but creating the asset needs a workspace.
The studio does the same thing without code. Open Models, choose Register, and pick local files, a job output, or a datastore. Then give it a name and review.

Then you manage its lifecycle. List and get let you inspect versions. For a model, only the description and tags can be updated, so a stage tag is the documented way to mark Prod or Staging. Any change to the files means a new version. Archive hides a version from default lists, but you can still use it.

Real companies keep separate dev, test and production workspaces. Azure M L registries decouple models, environments, and components from any one workspace, so you can develop in dev, publish to a registry, and deploy to endpoints elsewhere.
Next: real-time endpoints, where a registered version starts answering requests.
